column1: # Unification is the most fundamental thing core does after dispatch, and
# until this file existed no corpus row touched it. The reason was
# structural rather than an oversight: unify's clients — `is`, `case`,
# typed defs, record shapes — are all basic/lang-layer words, so a bare
# core registry called the unifier from nowhere, and core/spec's notation
# could name seven builtin type literals and no type CONSTRUCTOR at all.
# Two fixture words and three notation forms open it:
#   unifyq a b   the PREDICATE: did the two values unify — true or false.
#   meetq a b    the VALUE: the unified value itself, the MEET of the two,
#                or ERROR:fixture_no_meet when they do not unify.
#   d( … )       a disjunct of the listed items
#   [: T … ]     a typed list — child constraint, then retained elements
#   {: T k: v … }  a typed map, likewise
# Both words sit over core's own unifier (Go `UnifyR`, TS `unify`, Lean
# `unify`). For a long time there was only `unifyq`: core/ts had a flat
# predicate and no meet, so asking for the value would have pinned a port
# gap as a language contract. The predicate alone cannot tell `5 tor 6`
# from `5` as the answer to `d( 5 6 )` against `Integer`; the value rows
# at the end of this file can, and they are where the rules are stated.
# The answer is always the MORE SPECIFIC of the two: a concrete value over
# the type that admits it, a narrower type over a wider one.
# --- the shared subset: scalars, roots, plain containers -------------------
# Every one of these agreed on first measurement.
run unifyq { a: 1 b: 2 } { b: 2 a: 1 }
run unifyq { a: { b: 1 } } { a: { b: 1 } }
run unifyq { a: { b: 1 } } { a: { b: 2 } }
# A value unifies with a disjunct when some alternative admits it, and the
# answer is the value. A nested disjunct is an alternative like any other.

column3: whichever side the disjunct is on

column1: run unifyq 5 d( d( Integer ) String )
column3: a nested disjunct is walked, not compared

column1: run unifyq { a: 1 } d( Map List )
run unifyq true d( Integer String )

column3: the empty disjunct admits nothing

column1: # `[: T ]` and `{: T }` are TYPES. Against a plain container the child
# constrains every member; against each other the two children must unify.
# The elements a typed container RETAINS are not part of the type: two
# typed lists over one child unify whatever each retains.

column3: one element the child refuses is enough
two children with no meet
the retained elements are not compared
a disjunct child admits each element by some alternative

column1: run unifyq [: d( Integer String ) ] [: d( Boolean ) ]
column3: two disjunct children with no alternative in common

column1: run unifyq [: d( Integer String ) ] [: d( String Integer ) ]
column3: reordered alternatives are one disjunct

column1: run unifyq {: Integer a: 1 } {: Integer a: 1 }
# --- a ROOT type literal is not `Any` to a disjunct ------------------------
# `Any` keeps a disjunct whole; nothing else does. core/go asked "is the
# value's Parent() Any", which is a CARRIER's question: a bare literal's
# Parent() is its LATTICE parent, and Scalar, Node, Ideal, Word and Type
# all sit directly under Any — so each of them passed for Any, and
# `d( 'a' )` unified with `Node`, an empty disjunct with `Scalar`. Found
# by the Lean model's differential search (spec/tools/diff-fuzz.py). A root
# that DOES sit over an alternative narrows to it like any other type.

column3: the alternatives are walked, and none of them is a Type
Scalar sits over the Integer 0

column1: run unifyq d( Integer String ) Any
# The meet of two disjuncts is the disjunct of the pairwise meets of their
# alternatives; no pair unifying is no meet. (The kernel used to answer the
# FIRST alternative that matched — `Integer` for `Integer tor String`
run unifyq d( Integer String ) d( Integer String )
run unifyq d( Integer String ) d( String Integer )

column3: one pair in common is enough

column1: run unifyq d( Integer String ) d( 5 'a' )
run unifyq d( d( 5 6 ) String ) d( 5 6 )

column3: the same rule one level down

column1: run unifyq d( Integer String ) d( true none )
# Two MAP alternatives are two open patterns. Each admits any map carrying
# its keys, so both admit the maps carrying the keys of either: they meet
# as the two MERGED, whichever side each is on, and only a key both name
run unifyq d( { a: 1 } ) d( { a: 1 b: 2 } )
run unifyq d( { a: 1 b: 2 } ) d( { a: 1 } )
run unifyq d( { a: 1 } ) d( { b: 2 } )
column3: no key in common, so nothing to clash

column1: run unifyq d( { a: Integer } ) d( { a: 3 } )
run unifyq d( { a: 1 } ) d( { a: 2 } )
column3: a key both name must unify
a map alternative and a scalar one never meet

column1: # The EMPTY disjunct denotes the empty set, so it IS `Never`: it meets
# `Never` and another empty disjunct, and nothing else — not even `Any`.
run unifyq { a: d( ) } { a: Never }
column3: wherever it stands

column1: # The same rule with a set of one on the other side: a type against a
# disjunct meets EVERY alternative (`Integer` against `5 tor 6` is
# `5 tor 6`, where the kernel answered `5`), and a type no alternative
# meets has no meet. A list or a map HOLDING a type is a shape, not a
# value, and is treated the same way.
run unifyq Integer d( Integer String )
run unifyq d( Integer String ) Scalar
run unifyq d( Integer String ) Number

column3: a list holding a type is a shape
a typed container is a type

column1: run unifyq d( Integer String ) [: Integer ]
# A map alternative stays an open PATTERN: against a map VALUE it admits
# one carrying its keys, and against a map SHAPE the shape must carry the
run unifyq d( { a: 1 } { a: 2 } ) { a: 1 b: 2 }
column3: a value with an extra key

column1: run unifyq d( { a: 1 } { a: 2 } ) { a: Integer }
run unifyq d( { a: 1 } ) { a: Integer b: String }
run unifyq { a: Integer } d( { a: 1 } )
run unifyq d( { a: [q 1 ] } ) { a: [q Integer ] }
column3: a map holding a list that holds a type is a shape too

column1: run unifyq d( { a: 1 } ) { b: Integer }
column3: the shape lacks the key

column1: run unifyq d( { a: 1 } ) { a: String }
column3: the shape refuses the key
the value lacks the key

column1: # `meetq a b` is the unified value. Every rule above is restated here as the
# value it produces, because a predicate cannot tell a right answer from a
# wrong one that also happens to exist.
# Two values of one type are equal or have no meet. A type admits a value
# of it, and the VALUE is the meet. Of two types on one lattice chain the
# narrower is the meet. `Any` yields the other side — the none value
# included; the other degenerate roots unify only with themselves.

column3: a type against a value of it: the value
two types on one chain: the narrower
the None literal against the none value is the value
Never unifies only with Never

column1: # Element by element, at one length: each side narrows the other. The bare
# `List` literal — and `Node`, the family root over it — admits any list.

column3: each side narrows the other
two lengths never meet
an eval list is evaluated before it is unified

column1: # Two plain maps are CLOSED: a key only one side has stands as `Absent` on
# the other, which only a value admitting `Absent` unifies with — and a key
# whose meet is `Absent` is not in the result. Keys keep the LEFT map's
# order, then the right map's extras.
run meetq { a: Integer b: 2 } { a: 1 b: Integer }
run meetq { a: 1 b: 2 } { b: 2 a: 1 }
column3: the left map's key order

column1: run meetq { b: 2 a: 1 } { a: 1 b: 2 }
run meetq { a: { b: Integer } } { a: { b: 1 } }

column3: closed: a key only one side has is a mismatch

column1: run meetq { a: d( Integer Absent ) b: 1 } { b: 1 }
column3: unless its value admits Absent — and then the key is dropped

column1: run meetq { a: d( Integer Absent ) b: 1 } { b: 1 a: 5 }
# A typed container against a plain one is the PLAIN container, every
# member narrowed by the child. Two typed containers are the typed
# container over the meet of their children — and nothing else: what each

column3: a type element narrowed by the child stays a type
the meet of the two children
the retained elements are not part of the type

column1: run meetq [: d( Integer String ) ] [: d( String Integer ) ]

column3: two disjunct children meet as disjuncts do

column1: run meetq {: Integer a: 1 } {: Integer a: 1 }

column3: one surviving meet is that value, as a child too

column1: # The meet is the disjunct of the meets of the alternatives, reduced to its
# canonical form: repeats and absorbed alternatives dropped, the rest in
# the total order (core/spec/data.tsv pins that form). ONE surviving meet
# is that value, not a one-alternative disjunct.
run meetq d( Integer String ) d( Integer String )
column3: a disjunct with itself is itself — not its first alternative

column1: run meetq d( String Integer ) d( Integer String )
column3: the order the alternatives were written in decides nothing
one surviving meet is that value

column1: run meetq d( Integer String ) d( 5 6 )
column3: a type narrows to the values it admits

column1: run meetq d( Number String ) d( Integer Number )
column3: a meet absorbed by a wider meet is dropped

column1: run meetq d( d( 5 6 ) String ) d( 5 6 )
column3: a nested disjunct's meet is flattened into the result
a TYPE narrows every alternative, not the first

column1: run meetq d( Integer String ) Scalar
column3: a wider type keeps the disjunct

column1: run meetq d( Integer String ) Number
column3: a type admitting one alternative
a list holding a type is a shape, not a value
a VALUE is admitted by the first alternative that takes it

column1: run meetq d( Integer String ) Any
column3: against Any the disjunct stands whole

column1: # Map alternatives. Two patterns meet as the two merged — the left's keys,
# then the right's extras, a shared key holding the meet of its two
# values. A map VALUE is its own answer, extra keys and all. A map SHAPE
# is narrowed: each key the pattern names takes the meet, the rest stay.
run meetq d( { a: 1 } ) d( { a: 1 b: 2 } )
run meetq d( { a: 1 b: 2 } ) d( { a: 1 } )
run meetq d( { a: 1 } ) d( { b: 2 } )
run meetq d( { b: 2 } ) d( { a: 1 } )
column3: the left pattern's keys first

column1: run meetq d( { a: Integer } ) d( { a: 3 } )
column3: a shared key holds the meet of its two values

column1: run meetq d( { a: 1 } ) d( { a: 2 } )
run meetq d( { a: 1 } { b: 2 } ) d( { c: 3 } )
column3: every pair that merges is an alternative of the meet

column1: run meetq d( { a: 1 } { a: 2 } ) { a: 1 b: 2 }
column3: a value: the answer is the value

column1: run meetq d( { a: 1 } { a: 2 } ) { a: Integer }
column3: a shape: every alternative that fits narrows it

column1: run meetq d( { a: 1 } ) { a: Integer b: String }
column3: and the shape keeps its other keys

column1: run meetq d( { a: [q 1 ] } ) { a: [q Integer ] }
run meetq d( { a: 1 } ) { b: Integer }
